stimulus.text:
President Woodrow Wilson, Fourteen Points address to Congress, January 8, 1918 (verbatim excerpts):

"I. Open covenants of peace, openly arrived at, after which there shall be no private international understandings of any kind but diplomacy shall proceed always frankly and in the public view."

"II. Absolute freedom of navigation upon the seas, outside territorial waters, alike in peace and in war, except as the seas may be closed in whole or in part by international action for the enforcement of international covenants."

"III. The removal, so far as possible, of all economic barriers and the establishment of an equality of trade conditions among all the nations consenting to the peace and associating themselves for its maintenance."

"IV. Adequate guarantees given and taken that national armaments will be reduced to the lowest point consistent with domestic safety."

"XIV. A general association of nations must be formed under specific covenants for the purpose of affording mutual guarantees of political independence and territorial integrity to great and small states alike."

options.text: only the League of Nations survived from Wilson's plan into the Treaty of Versailles
the Allies adopted Wilson's call for open diplomacy and free trade in full
options.misconception: The Allies did not adopt open diplomacy or free trade in full. The treaty imposed harsh terms on Germany and kept the victors' colonial empires intact.

options.text: Germany was invited to negotiate the treaty's terms as an equal
options.misconception: Germany was not invited to negotiate. The treaty was presented to German delegates, who were told to sign or face invasion.

options.text: Wilson abandoned the League of Nations at the Paris Peace Conference
options.misconception: Wilson fought for the League at Paris and won its inclusion in the treaty. He refused to give it up even when the rest of his plan was set aside.

rationales.A: Background from the books: the European Allies set aside most of Wilson's points in favor of a punitive peace, but the League of Nations was written into the Treaty of Versailles. The League was the one part of the plan that survived.
rationales.B: The Allies did not adopt open diplomacy or free trade in full. The treaty imposed harsh terms on Germany and kept the victors' colonial empires intact.
rationales.C: Germany was not invited to negotiate. The treaty was presented to German delegates, who were told to sign or face invasion.
rationales.D: Wilson fought for the League at Paris and won its inclusion in the treaty. He refused to give it up even when the rest of his plan was set aside.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what Wilson's plan promised. Open diplomacy, free trade, lower arms, self-determination, and a league of nations.
2. Ask what the settlement delivered. Background from the books: the Allies imposed a punitive peace on Germany and kept their empires, but they accepted the League.
3. Compare the two lists. Only the League appears on both.
Remember: to judge how much of a plan survived, list what the plan promised and cross off what the settlement dropped.
